# Framework Development and Results {#sec-chapter4}

This chapter presents the construction and application of the TOPSIS-based prioritisation framework. It covers data preparation, indicator normalisation and weight assignment, TOPSIS computation and ranking, and sensitivity analysis, before discussing the substantive interpretation of the results. The complete Python implementation is provided in Appendix A. All code referenced in this chapter can be executed directly to reproduce the outputs shown here.

## Data Preparation

The dataset covers five IT services drawn from the trading IT division of the case organisation, extracted from its ITSM instance. Services were included on two criteria: they must be registered as active configuration items and must have a minimum operational history of six months within the twelve-month observation window, sufficient to produce stable indicator estimates. Services with fewer than three recorded production changes during the window were assigned the portfolio mean for CFR, consistent with the imputation approach recommended for sparse operational datasets [@grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019]. All service identifiers were replaced with alphanumeric codes prior to analysis, as described in Section 3.2.1. No team, vendor or individual identifiers are present in the dataset.

The four indicators are operationally defined as follows, consistent with the definitions established in Section 3.1.4. Incident frequency is the total number of P2 and P3 incidents attributed to the service during the observation window, divided by service age in months. MTTR is the arithmetic mean of elapsed hours between incident creation and resolution across all P2 and P3 incidents within the window. CFR is the proportion of production changes that resulted in an unplanned rollback or a subsequent incident within 72 hours of deployment. Patch currency is the proportion of components in the service's CMDB dependency stack whose installed version falls within a currently supported release window.

Incident frequency, MTTR and CFR are cost criteria, for which lower values indicate lower technical debt severity. Patch currency is a benefit criterion, for which higher values are preferable.

## Indicator Normalisation and Weighting

Before aggregation, each indicator is normalised using vector normalisation to remove differences in scale and unit:

$$r_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{m} x_{ij}^2}}$$

Vector normalisation is preferred over min-max normalisation because it preserves proportional relationships between values without compressing the range to a fixed interval, a property that [@grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019] recommend for composite indicators where extreme values carry substantive meaning. A service with an unusually high MTTR should retain its full distance from lower-performing services in the normalised space rather than be pulled toward a truncated maximum. A weighted normalised matrix is then constructed by multiplying each normalised value by its criterion weight:

$$v_{ij} = w_j \cdot r_{ij}$$

Two weight configurations are applied. The baseline equal-weight configuration assigns $w_j = 0.25$ to each criterion and serves as the reference case against which the differential configuration is evaluated. The differential configuration assigns higher weights to MTTR and CFR.

This reflects a design judgement rather than a claim attributable to a single empirical source, and it is grounded in three converging observations from the literature. First, @ramasubbuManagingTechnicalDebt2015 establish that technical debt in COTS enterprise systems increases the probability of system failures by up to 62 percent, identifying incident frequency as the most directly observable TD signal in vendor-platform environments. This makes the speed of recovery from those incidents, captured by MTTR, the dimension most consequential to operational governance once a failure has occurred. Second, Nord, Ozkaya and Woody (2021) classify delivery tempo degradation and deployment instability explicitly as observable symptoms from which technical debt can be detected and prioritised in production environments [@nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021]. This provides direct grounding for elevating the weights of both MTTR and CFR relative to the remaining two criteria. Third, Fungprasertkul, Bahsoon and Kazman (2024) establish that TD dimensions can and should be assigned differential weights to reflect the perspectives of different stakeholders and the operational context in which monitoring takes place [@fungprasertkulTechnicalDebtMonitoring2024], offering methodological precedent for a two-configuration design in which the baseline equal-weight case is tested against a configuration calibrated to domain context.



Two weight configurations are applied, as specified in @sec-frameworkdesign. The baseline equal-weight configuration assigns $w_j = 0.25$ to each criterion and serves as the reference case. The differential configuration assigns higher weights to MTTR and CFR, reflecting their higher operational salience in a trading environment where speed of recovery and deployment stability directly determine financial exposure [@forsgrenAccelerate2018]. The differential weights are $w_{\text{MTTR}} = w_{\text{CFR}} = 0.30$ and $w_{\text{IncFreq}} = w_{\text{Patch}} = 0.20$.

| Configuration | Incident Freq. | MTTR | CFR  | Patch Currency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal (baseline) | 0.25 | 0.25 | 0.25 | 0.25 |
| Differential | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.30 | 0.20 |
